blogs.title: From Right-to-Control to Fraudulent-Inducement: The Fifth Circuit’s Post-Ciminelli Roadmap in Securities Fraud
blogs.description: This post unpacks how the Fifth Circuit leverages Kousisis to distinguish impermissible right-to-control theories from a viable fraudulent-inducement theory under 18 U.S.C. § 1348. It explains why inducing investors, via misrepresentations, to part with money for securities alleges deprivation of traditional property—sidestepping Ciminelli’s bar on convictions premised solely on lost “valuable economic information.” It also explores what the opinion signals about charging strategies in financial fraud cases after Ciminelli.

blogs.title: No Net-Loss Needed: Intent to Profit as Intent to Defraud in Pump-and-Dump Prosecutions
blogs.description: Focusing on the opinion’s reliance on Kousisis, this piece examines the Fifth Circuit’s rejection of a “victim-loss” prerequisite. It analyzes why the alleged profit-seeking pump-and-dump scheme satisfies § 1348’s intent-to-defraud element even if investors received market-priced shares. The post highlights the court’s treatment of injury at the indictment stage and discusses the broader implications for trading schemes where defendants argue there was no net pecuniary harm.

blogs.title: Criminal § 1348 as Mail/Wire Fraud’s Twin: Doctrinal Borrowing and the Edges of Overlap with Rule 10b-5
blogs.description: This analysis situates § 1348 within the mail and wire fraud family, showing how the Fifth Circuit imports concepts like “scheme to defraud” and “intent to defraud.” It compares § 1348’s elements to civil and criminal Rule 10b-5, noting practical differences (e.g., no reliance requirement in criminal § 1348, conspiracy and aiding/abetting tools) that make § 1348 attractive to prosecutors. It also flags potential overbreadth and fair-notice concerns as courts increasingly treat § 1348 like a general fraud statute in securities markets.

blogs.title: Influencer Hype Meets Criminal Fraud: Speech, Social Media, and the Line Between Puffs and Deception
blogs.description: Looking beyond the procedural posture, this post considers the opinion’s implications for social-media-driven market activity. It discusses how misstatements about positions and price predictions can become criminally actionable when tied to a scheme to induce purchases under false pretenses. The piece previews possible First Amendment friction, compliance risks for online traders and “finfluencers,” and what disclosures or practices may mitigate exposure in light of the Fifth Circuit’s embrace of fraudulent inducement.
